University of Michigan's final November sentiment index rose to 51.5 from 48 in October, just shy of the 51.6 Bloomberg consensus.

One year ahead inflation expectations dropped to 3.7% from 4.7% in October, the lowest since February; long run expectations eased to 3.3%.

The survey ran Oct. 20 to Nov. 16, a window that included midterms in which Democrats took the House and Senate and flipped governorships in Georgia, Iowa, Texas, Ohio and Nevada.

What moved the index

Consumer mood improved in November, with the University of Michigan's final sentiment reading ticking up to 51.5 from 48 the month before, a hair under economists' 51.6 median call. Assessments of both present conditions and the outlook strengthened, and a measure of personal finances reached its best level since July.

Lower prices at the pump helped. The national average for a gallon of gasoline started the month above 4 dollars, per AAA, and had fallen to about 3.75 dollars by the time the survey wrapped.

Politics, prices and expectations

The survey period spanned the midterm elections, when Democrats captured the House and the Senate and turned governorships in Georgia, Iowa, Texas, Ohio and Nevada. The contest centered on the economy and affordability, and Democrats' sweeping win partly reflected voter frustration with elevated costs for groceries, fuel, medical care and housing.

Price fears eased noticeably. Households now see inflation running at 3.7% over the next year, down from 4.7% in October and the lowest reading since February. They peg longer run inflation at 3.3% for the coming five to 10 years, also a step down from last month.

"Consumers appear to anticipate potential changes to public policy under a divided government to come," said Joanne Hsu, the survey's director. "Accordingly, the expectations index surged for independents." After the election, expectations for gas prices fell and are now "broadly comparable to pre-Iran readings," Hsu added.

The backdrop investors care about

Even with the improvement, the picture is still mixed. Economists estimate consumer prices were up about 4% year over year in October, and borrowing remains expensive, with 30 year mortgage rates holding above 7% since mid September. Earlier this year, relentless price increases pushed the gauge to its lowest level on record in May, and in October it registered the second weakest reading ever.

The bottom line: softer gasoline prices and cooling inflation expectations can support spending-sensitive names, but higher financing costs still bite rate exposed sectors. Keep an eye on how these crosscurrents show up in holiday sales and credit metrics.

Anthropic has gone public at a valuation of about $1.5 trillion, while Amazon went public in 1997 at around $440 million. Anthropic has about $33 billion in revenue this year and no profit, and investors are paying more than 40 times its sales, against about 3 times for Amazon. Briefs Finance CEO Jaspreet Singh says nobody knows what comes next, and that long-term investors use downturns to buy instead of panic selling.

Tech stocks are selling off because investors don't know who will lead Nvidia, the company that has been funding the AI industry and selling it chips.

Inflation has the Federal Reserve planning to raise interest rates, with a hike expected in December, and that puts pressure on homebuyers, private equity and the $40 trillion national debt.

Briefs Finance CEO Jaspreet Singh says nobody has a crystal ball, so his rules are to buy when markets are low, hold long term and invest only what you're willing to lose.

The national debt is above $40 trillion, and the Federal Reserve has gone from sending Washington its profits to losing money.

President Trump's four-part plan leans on shorter-term debt, stablecoin companies buying Treasuries, a bigger balance sheet and government stakes in private companies.

The goal is to outgrow the debt, not pay it off, so Jaspreet Singh points investors to the seven industries where Washington wants growth.

The Fed makes its next rate decision on December 9 and is now talking about jumbo interest rate hikes of 0.5%, though one in December looks unlikely.

Washington will pay a record $1.05 trillion in interest this year on $40 trillion of debt, and that debt resets at higher rates as the Fed hikes.

Jaspreet Singh's five moves are to pay down variable-rate debt, earn interest on your savings, know which stocks feel the pressure, look at value and hedge.

Margin debt, the money investors borrow to buy stocks, is at a record of around 4.6% of GDP, up from 3.9% in 2021.

ETF money has more than tripled in five years to 7% of GDP, while corporate buybacks and 401(k) money sit below their earlier peaks.

Margin calls and panic selling can make the next downturn deeper, so Jaspreet Singh keeps buying broad market funds and says most investors should skip margin debt.

Jensen Huang is out at Nvidia over affairs with multiple people, and the company he founded has been the bank of American AI, with about $30 billion into OpenAI and $10 billion into Anthropic.

A hotter-than-expected inflation report has Fed officials talking about a possible 0.5% hike in December, and gold, silver, and bitcoin fell on the news.

President Trump said the US may not need a deal with Iran, keeping oil prices and inflation risk high. Jaspreet Singh breaks down what it all means for AI stocks and your portfolio.

Stocks are booming at the fastest pace in years, jobless claims just hit a 57-year low, and most investors still feel like nobody is hiring.

The Fed is protecting the dollar over the economy, oil swings on every Iran headline, and a few AI companies are carrying an S&P 500 where four of five stocks sit in a correction.

Jaspreet Singh explains why circular financing between Nvidia, OpenAI, Anthropic, and SpaceX rhymes with 2008's house of cards, and how his three investing pillars handle a stock market bubble.

The Fed has raised rates, cut them, then raised them again only twice in the last 60 years, and both times the economy fell into a recession and stocks crashed.

The same stop-and-go cycle is playing out now, with one big difference: US debt is 125% of GDP today versus about 30% in 1980.

In the 1970s gold rose roughly 24x, real estate 157%, stocks lagged, and cash lost half its value. Jaspreet Singh lays out five assets to consider before the next flip.

The IRS 2027 tax plan keeps the same seven rates but widens every bracket and lifts the married-filing-jointly standard deduction to $33,200.

The 0% long-term capital gains bracket rises to $102,100, so a household living on $135,300 of investment income could owe $0 in federal income tax.

C corporations still pay 21%, small businesses keep the 20% QBI deduction, and the 401(k) limit climbs to $25,500 with an $8,500 catch-up for investors over 50.
